title: Why Sailors Poured Oil on Storm Waves #shorts

lines.text: Sailors in giant storms used to fight thirty foot waves by pouring oil on the water. And it actually worked.
Picture a captain in a storm, waves smashing over the deck, and he yells, "Get the fish oil!"
The crew fills canvas bags with oil, pokes holes in them, and hangs them over the side.
The new guy says, "Captain, we're sinking, and you're cooking?"
But slowly, all around the ship, the water goes smooth, like somebody ironed it.
The waves are still huge, but they stop breaking over the ship.
One inventor was so obsessed with this, he carried oil hidden inside his walking stick.
He'd walk up to a windy pond, pour out one teaspoon, and half an acre of water went flat.
People thought it was a magic trick. He just shrugged.
You see, wind makes big waves by grabbing tiny ripples first.
Oil spreads into a film so thin it's only one molecule thick, and it wipes those ripples out.
It's like trying to push a car on ice. No grip, no push, no wave.
So for hundreds of years, one of the best pieces of storm gear on a ship was basically a leaky bag of salad dressing.
